title: 1789: the Revolution proclaims liberty and equality
refs: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
text:
To understand the Republic, we need to go back to the French Revolution.

In 1789, France is a kingdom. King Louis XVI is an [absolute monarch]: he has all the power. Society is unequal: nobles and clergy have [privileges], while ordinary people pay almost all the taxes.

In spring 1789, the people's representatives meet in Versailles. On 17 June, they declare themselves the [National Assembly]: they say that power comes from the people, not from the king.

On 14 July 1789, the people of Paris storm the Bastille, a prison that stands for the king's power. On the night of 4 August, privileges are abolished.

On 26 August 1789, the Assembly adopts the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Its first article says: "Men are born and remain free and equal in rights."

This text proclaims new ideas: freedom of opinion and expression, equality before the law, and the sovereignty of the nation. It is still part of the French Constitution today!

In 1789, France is not yet a republic: it still has a king. But the great ideas of the future Republic have been born.

This is also when the blue, white and red cockade appears, the ancestor of the French flag.

title: The birth of the First Republic
refs: Proclamation of the abolition of the monarchy
text:
In 1791, King Louis XVI tries to escape abroad. He is arrested at Varennes. Many French people no longer trust him. In 1792, France is at war with foreign kings.

On 10 August 1792, the people of Paris attack the Tuileries Palace, where the king lives. The [monarchy] falls.

A new assembly is elected: the Convention. For the first time, all men can vote, rich or poor.

On 21 September 1792, the Convention abolishes royalty. On 22 September 1792, official documents start to be dated "Year I of the Republic". The First French [Republic] is born!

In a republic, there is no king. Power belongs to the people, who choose their representatives.

The Republic adopts symbols we still know today:
- the tricolour flag;
- La Marseillaise, a war song written in 1792;
- a woman wearing a Phrygian cap, who stands for Liberty, and who will later be called Marianne.

But this first Republic also has very dark moments, like the Terror (1793–1794), when thousands of people are executed.

In 1799, General Bonaparte takes power. The First Republic will soon disappear.

It will take almost a century for the Republic to settle in for good!

title: Napoleon I, Emperor of the French
text:
In 1799, General Napoleon Bonaparte seizes power in a [coup d'état]. He becomes First Consul.

On 2 December 1804, in Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, he is crowned Emperor of the French as Napoleon I. The painter David showed the ceremony in a huge painting. This is the end of the First Republic: France becomes an [empire].

Napoleon keeps some ideas from the Revolution. In 1804, he publishes the Civil Code, which says everyone is equal before the law. He creates lycées (high schools), prefects and the Legion of Honour.

But he rules alone, like an absolute monarch. There is no real freedom of the press any more: newspapers are watched. Elections are almost meaningless. In 1802, he even brings back slavery in the colonies.

Napoleon goes to war with almost all of Europe. His armies win great victories, like Austerlitz in 1805, but these wars kill hundreds of thousands of people.

In 1812, he suffers a terrible defeat in Russia. In 1815, he is beaten at Waterloo and exiled to a tiny, remote island in the Atlantic Ocean, Saint Helena, where he dies in 1821.

This period shows that one man can take all the power, even after a revolution made in the name of freedom.

title: The kings come back
text:
After Napoleon's fall, kings return to France. This is called the [Restoration].

Louis XVI's brother becomes king as Louis XVIII. He doesn't want to go all the way back to the past: he accepts a Charter, which guarantees some freedoms and equality before the law. There is an elected assembly, but only the richest men can vote: about 100,000 people out of 30 million French people!

The tricolour flag is replaced by the kings' white flag.

In 1824, his other brother, Charles X, becomes king. He is much more authoritarian. He wants to give power back to the nobility and the Church. He is crowned at Reims, like the kings of old.

In July 1830, Charles X issues orders that abolish freedom of the press and cut the number of voters even further. Parisians are furious...

Throughout this period, many French people remain attached to the ideas of the Revolution. Songs, newspapers and secret societies dream of bringing back the Republic.

title: The Three Glorious Days
text:
In July 1830, King Charles X wants to abolish freedom of the press. Journalists protest, then the workers and students of Paris rise up.

For three days, 27, 28 and 29 July 1830, Parisians build [barricades] in the streets with paving stones, carts and furniture. They fight the king's soldiers. These three days are called the "Three Glorious Days".

Charles X has to give up his throne and flee to England. But the Republic is not proclaimed: the deputies choose a new king, Louis-Philippe. He is no longer called "King of France", but "King of the French". This is called the [July Monarchy].

The tricolour flag becomes France's flag again, and it will never change again!

The painter Eugène Delacroix showed this revolution in a very famous painting: Liberty Leading the People. It shows a woman, Liberty, wearing a Phrygian cap and holding up the tricolour flag above a barricade. The painting is now in the Louvre.

But under Louis-Philippe, still only rich men can vote: about 250,000 voters. Many French people are waiting for more change.

It is also in 1830 that the French army conquers Algiers: this is the beginning of the [colonisation] of Algeria.

title: 1848: the Second Republic and universal suffrage
text:
In 1848, many French people are unhappy. There is an economic crisis: bread is expensive and many workers are unemployed. And still only rich men are allowed to vote.

In February 1848, Parisians rise up again and build barricades. King Louis-Philippe [abdicates|abdicate] and flees to England. On 24 February 1848, the Second Republic is proclaimed.

The new government makes big decisions:
- [universal suffrage] for men: all men over 21 can vote, rich or poor. The number of voters jumps from about 250,000 to 9 million!
- freedom of the press and of assembly;
- the abolition of slavery in the colonies;
- the end of the death penalty for political crimes.

The poet Alphonse de Lamartine, a member of the government, refuses to let the red flag replace the tricolour. He explains that the tricolour "has travelled around the world with the Republic and the Empire".

But women still don't have the right to vote.

In December 1848, the French elect a President of the Republic by universal suffrage for the first time. It is Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte, the nephew of Napoleon I...

title: Slavery is abolished for good
text:
In France's colonies in the Caribbean (Guadeloupe, Martinique), in French Guiana and on Réunion Island, hundreds of thousands of people from Africa or born to African parents are held in [slavery]. They are bought and sold, and forced to work on sugar cane plantations.

The Revolution had abolished slavery in 1794, but Napoleon brought it back in 1802.

One man fights for years to end it: Victor Schœlcher. The son of a porcelain maker, he travelled to the Caribbean and was deeply shocked by what he saw. He writes books and articles to denounce slavery.

In 1848, he joins the government of the Second Republic. On 27 April 1848, a [decree] abolishes slavery for good in all French colonies. It declares that "French soil can no longer bear slaves".

About 250,000 people become free and become French citizens. The men even get the right to vote!

On some islands, enslaved people had already risen up and won their freedom before the news arrived.

Today, every year on 10 May, France remembers slavery and its abolition. And since 2001, a law recognises that slavery was a [crime against humanity].

Victor Schœlcher is buried in the Panthéon in Paris, where the nation honours its great figures.

title: Napoleon III and the Second Empire
text:
Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte was elected President of the Republic in 1848. But the Constitution doesn't allow him to run again. He doesn't want to give up power.

On 2 December 1851, he carries out a coup d'état: he has deputies arrested and dissolves the Assembly. Republicans who resist are killed, imprisoned or exiled. The writer Victor Hugo has to flee and lives in exile for almost 19 years.

A year later, on 2 December 1852, Louis-Napoleon becomes emperor as Napoleon III. This is the Second Empire. The Second Republic lasted only four years.

During the Second Empire, men still vote, but elections are watched and newspapers controlled. The police keep an eye on opponents.

France modernises a lot:
- railways spread across the whole country;
- Baron Haussmann transforms Paris with wide boulevards, parks and sewers;
- department stores and banks appear.

France also enlarges its colonial empire, in Africa and Asia.

In 1870, Napoleon III declares war on Prussia (which will become Germany). It is a disaster...

title: Defeat at Sedan and the birth of the Third Republic
text:
In July 1870, France goes to war with Prussia. The French army is badly prepared.

On 2 September 1870, at Sedan, the French army is surrounded and Emperor Napoleon III is taken prisoner! This is the end of the Second Empire.

On 4 September 1870, at Paris City Hall, republican deputies, including Léon Gambetta, proclaim the Third Republic in front of an excited crowd.

But the war goes on. The German armies besiege Paris. Parisians suffer from cold and hunger: in the end they eat dogs, cats, rats and even the elephants from the zoo!

On 7 October 1870, Léon Gambetta leaves besieged Paris... in a balloon! He flies over the enemy lines to organise resistance in the rest of the country. Dozens of balloons leave Paris during the siege, carrying people, letters and carrier pigeons.

In January 1871, France has to sign an [armistice]. It loses Alsace and part of Lorraine, which remain German until 1918. It is a great trauma for the French.

The Third Republic is born in defeat, and at first nobody knows whether it will last. Yet it will last 70 years, longer than any regime since 1789!

title: The Paris Commune
text:
After the defeat by Germany, in February 1871, the French elect a new Assembly. Most of its members are [monarchists], meaning they want a king back. It settles in Versailles.

Parisians, however, are very republican. They suffered during the siege and feel betrayed.

On 18 March 1871, the government tries to take back the Paris National Guard's cannons on the hill of Montmartre. Parisians resist. This starts a revolt: the [Paris Commune].

Parisians elect their own council. The Commune makes decisions that are ahead of their time: separating the Churches from the State, free non-religious schools, a ban on night work for bakers. Women play a big role, like the teacher Louise Michel.

But the Versailles government, led by Adolphe Thiers, sends in the army. From 21 to 28 May 1871, during the "Bloody Week", the soldiers retake Paris street by street. The fighting is terrible: thousands of Communards are killed, often shot without trial. The Communards, for their part, execute hostages and set fire to buildings, like the Tuileries Palace.

Thousands of Communards are then imprisoned or [deported|deport] to New Caledonia, like Louise Michel.

The Commune remains a painful memory. It shows that France is still deeply divided about what form the Republic should take.

title: The Republic by a single vote
text:
After the Commune, the National Assembly is dominated by monarchists. They would like to bring back a king. But they can't agree on who!

Charles X's grandson, the Count of Chambord, could become king. But he refuses to accept the tricolour flag: he wants the kings' white flag. Many French people refuse to go back in time like that. This quarrel makes the monarchists lose time.

In 1875, the Assembly has to vote laws to organise power. On 30 January 1875, a deputy, Henri Wallon, proposes an [amendment] saying that the head of state will be called "President of the Republic" and elected for seven years.

The vote is extremely close: 353 votes for, 352 against. The Republic is adopted... by a single vote! That is why Wallon is sometimes called the "father of the Republic".

The [constitutional laws] of 1875 organise the Third Republic:
- a Chamber of Deputies, elected by universal male suffrage;
- a Senate;
- a President of the Republic, elected by the deputies and senators.

At the following elections, the republicans win the majority. By 1879, they control all the institutions. The Republic is finally here to stay!

This story shows that every single vote counts.

title: La Marseillaise and 14 July
text:
Once in power, the republicans want all French people to feel attached to the Republic. To do this, they choose symbols that recall the Revolution.

In 1879, Parliament leaves Versailles, the city of kings, and returns to Paris.

On 14 February 1879, La Marseillaise becomes the [national anthem]. The song was written in 1792 by Rouget de Lisle for the soldiers of the Army of the Rhine, then sung by volunteers from Marseille as they marched to Paris. It had been banned under the Empire and the kings.

On 6 July 1880, a law makes 14 July the [national holiday]. It recalls both the storming of the Bastille in 1789 and the Festival of the Federation in 1790, which celebrated the unity of the French people.

14 July 1880 is celebrated all over France: parades, dances, banquets, illuminations, tricolour flags at the windows. A great military parade takes place in Paris, at Longchamp.

Since then, every year on 14 July, there is a military parade in Paris, public dances and fireworks all over France.

Singing La Marseillaise and celebrating 14 July was a way of making the French love the Republic, especially those who lived in the countryside.

title: Marianne and the motto in every town
text:
In the 1880s, the republicans want the Republic to be visible everywhere, even in the smallest village.

The [motto] "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity", born during the Revolution, is carved on the front of town halls, schools and public buildings.

Marianne becomes the symbol of the Republic. She is a woman who often wears a Phrygian cap, a red cap that freed slaves wore in ancient times: it is the symbol of liberty. Sometimes she has a crown of laurel leaves or ears of wheat.

A bust of Marianne is placed in almost every town hall in France. Why "Marianne"? It was a very common name among ordinary people in the 18th century. Giving this name to the Republic was a way of saying that it belonged to everyone.

Big statues of the Republic are also built. In Paris, on the Place de la République, a huge statue of Marianne is unveiled in 1883. Around her, three statues stand for Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.

In every town, the town hall becomes an important place of the Republic: people vote there, get married there and register births there. Since 1884, the mayor has been elected by the town council, which is itself elected by the inhabitants.

Today, you can find Marianne on stamps, coins and the government's logo.

title: Freedom of the press and freedom of assembly
refs: Law on the Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881
text:
Under the Empire and the kings, newspapers were watched. Sometimes you needed permission to publish, and you could be punished for criticising the government.

The republicans want to guarantee the freedoms promised by the Declaration of the Rights of Man of 1789.

On 30 June 1881, a law establishes [freedom of assembly]: citizens can gather to discuss things without asking for permission.

On 29 July 1881, a major law establishes [freedom of the press]. It begins: "Printing and bookselling are free." Anyone can start a newspaper without permission. People can criticise the government, draw cartoons and defend their ideas.

This law also sets limits: you are not allowed to lie in order to damage someone's reputation (this is called [defamation]), or to insult people. Later, a ban on inciting hatred or violence will be added.

Thanks to this law, hundreds of newspapers appear. Newspapers become very cheap and very popular. Some sell more than a million copies a day!

In 1884, another law allows [trade unions], which let workers group together to defend their rights.

The 1881 law still exists today. Freedom of expression is one of the most important freedoms in a democracy: it allows everyone to give their opinion.

title: A new colonial empire
text:
At the end of the 19th century, European countries set out to conquer territories in Africa and Asia. This is [colonisation]. France had already begun conquering Algeria in 1830.

Under the Third Republic, France greatly enlarges its colonial empire:
- in 1881, it imposes a protectorate on Tunisia;
- in the 1880s, it conquers Indochina (today Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia);
- it conquers a large part of West and Central Africa;
- in 1896, it takes Madagascar.

Around 1900, the French colonial empire is the second largest in the world, after the British Empire.

Jules Ferry, who also made the school laws, strongly supports colonisation. He says that "superior races" have a duty to "civilise" "inferior races". Today we know this idea is false and racist: there are no superior races. Even at the time, some deputies, like Georges Clemenceau, opposed it.

Colonisation is often carried out through war. The colonised peoples lose their freedom and their land. They don't have the same rights as the French: they are subject to unfair rules, sometimes have to do forced labour, and cannot vote.

This is a huge contradiction: the Republic proclaims liberty and equality in France, but does not grant them to the peoples it colonises.

Most colonies will become independent after 1945, often after wars, as in Algeria in 1962.

title: The Eiffel Tower celebrates the centenary of 1789
text:
In 1889, it has been a hundred years since the French Revolution began. The Republic wants to celebrate this [centenary] in a spectacular way.

Paris holds a World's Fair: a huge event where countries from all over the world show off their inventions, machines and products. More than 32 million visitors come!

For the occasion, the engineer Gustave Eiffel and his team build an iron tower 300 metres tall. At the time, it is the tallest structure in the world! It is built in just two years, with 18,000 iron parts and 2.5 million rivets.

At first, many artists hate it. They find it ugly and call it a "skeleton of a belfry" or a "tower of Babel". It was supposed to stand for only twenty years... But it has become the symbol of Paris and of France all over the world!

The tower shows the power of French industry and science. For the republicans, the Republic stands for progress and modernity.

The 1889 fair also shows off the colonial empire, with pavilions presenting the colonies. People from the colonies are even put on display in a humiliating way, as in a zoo. Today we find this shocking and racist.

Today, the Eiffel Tower welcomes millions of visitors every year. With its antennas, it is now about 330 metres tall.

title: The Republic turns one hundred
Jules Ferry: free, compulsory and secular school
text:
Around 1880, many children don't go to school, or hardly ever. In the countryside, they work in the fields; in towns, some work in factories. Many schools charge fees, and some are run by the Church. Millions of adults can't read or write well.

Jules Ferry, the Minister of Public Instruction, believes the Republic needs educated citizens who can vote wisely. He passes two great laws:

- the law of 16 June 1881 makes state primary school [free]: families no longer have to pay anything;
- the law of 28 March 1882 makes education [compulsory] for all children, boys and girls, aged 6 to 13. It also makes state school [secular]: religion is no longer taught there. It is replaced by "moral and civic instruction".

On Thursdays, schools are closed so that families who wish can send their children to religious classes.

In 1886, another law says that teachers in state schools must no longer be members of religious orders, but secular [teachers].

All over France, towns build schools. Many villages have a "town hall school": a single building with the town hall in the middle, the boys' school on one side and the girls' school on the other. You can still see them today!

Girls go to school too: in 1880, a law even creates high schools for girls.

School becomes the place where you learn to read, write and count... and to become a citizen of the Republic.

title: The "black hussars" of the Republic
A school day in Jules Ferry's time
refs: Le Tour de la France par deux enfants
text:
Imagine a school day around 1890...

Boys and girls are in separate schools or classes. Pupils wear a black or grey smock to protect their clothes. They sit on wooden benches, at desks with a hole for the [inkwell].

In the morning, the teacher writes a moral saying on the blackboard, for example: "Do right and let people talk." The pupils copy it out.

To write, they use a pen holder with a metal nib that they dip into purple ink. Watch out for blots! They also write on a slate with chalk. Exercise books must be very neat.

On the timetable: reading, writing, arithmetic, dictation, history, geography with big wall maps, "object lessons" (science), singing, gymnastics, and "moral and civic instruction". Girls also learn sewing.

The most famous reading book is called The Tour of France by Two Children. It tells the story of two brothers, André and Julien, who leave Lorraine, which has become German, and travel around France. They discover the regions, the trades and great people. Millions of children read it!

Discipline is strict. Good pupils receive "good points" and picture cards. Pupils who are punished sometimes have to wear a dunce's cap or write lines. Raps on the fingers with a ruler happened, even though they were forbidden.

Heat comes from a wood stove in the middle of the classroom. In winter, each pupil sometimes brings a log!

title: The school certificate, a family's pride
text:
At the end of primary school, at about 12, the best pupils take an exam: the [primary school certificate], often called the "certif".

The exam takes place in another school, often in the main town of the district, in front of examiners the children don't know. For them, it is a big, slightly scary day!

Here are the tests:
- a dictation: more than five mistakes and you fail!
- arithmetic problems, with trains passing each other and taps filling bathtubs;
- a composition;
- questions on history, geography and science;
- singing, drawing and, for girls, sewing.

Passing the certificate is a huge source of pride for the child, the family and the teacher. The diploma is often framed and hung on the wall at home. In the evening, there is sometimes a party in the village.

For many children, it is the end of their schooling: afterwards they go to work, in the fields, the factory or the workshop, or as apprentices. Only a few go on to secondary school.

Thanks to the Republic's schools, almost all French people can read and write by the beginning of the 20th century. School also allowed children from modest families to become teachers, civil servants or engineers.

The school certificate was abolished in 1989. Today, school is compulsory in France from age 3 to 16.

title: The Dreyfus affair and "J'accuse…!"
text:
In 1894, a French army captain, Alfred Dreyfus, is accused of handing military secrets to Germany. He is Jewish, and at the time [antisemitism], hatred of Jews, is widespread.

He is tried in secret and convicted without real evidence. He is publicly stripped of his rank in front of a crowd: his stripes are torn off and his sword is broken, while he cries: "I am innocent! Long live France!" He is sent to a prison colony on Devil's Island, in French Guiana.

Later, it is discovered that the real culprit is another officer, Esterhazy. But in January 1898, the army acquits him and refuses to admit its mistake.

On 13 January 1898, the great writer Émile Zola publishes an open letter to the President of the Republic in the newspaper L'Aurore, with a huge headline: "J'accuse…!" ("I accuse…!"). He accuses the army chiefs of convicting an innocent man and protecting a guilty one. Zola is convicted and has to go into exile in England.

France is torn into two camps: the Dreyfusards, who defend justice and truth, and the anti-Dreyfusards, who think the army's honour must be protected. Families argue at the dinner table!

In 1898, Dreyfusards found the Human Rights League. Dreyfus is finally declared innocent in 1906.

The Dreyfus affair shows the importance of [freedom of expression] and of the press: thanks to newspapers, citizens were able to expose an injustice. It also shows that justice must be the same for everyone, whatever their religion.

title: The separation of the Churches and the State
refs: 1905 French law on the Separation of the Churches and the State
text:
Since Napoleon, the French state had paid priests, pastors and rabbis, and appointed bishops. The Catholic religion had a very important place in public life.

After the schools, the republicans want to separate religion and the state completely.

On 9 December 1905, a law prepared by the deputy Aristide Briand establishes the separation of the Churches and the State. Its first two articles are very important:
- article 1: the Republic ensures [freedom of conscience] and guarantees the free practice of religion. Everyone is free to believe or not to believe, and to practise the religion of their choice;
- article 2: the Republic does not recognise, pay or fund any religion. The state favours no religion.

This is called [secularism] (laïcité in French). The state is neutral: it is neither for nor against religions.

At first, the law causes big arguments. The Catholic Church protests. When officials come to make inventories of objects in churches, worshippers sometimes resist, occasionally violently.

Then, little by little, the law is applied peacefully. Churches built before 1905 belong to the towns, which look after them, and believers can use them.

Today, secularism is one of the principles of the Republic. In state schools, teachers are neutral, and every pupil is respected, whatever their religion or beliefs.

title: The Popular Front and paid holidays
text:
In the 1930s, a severe economic crisis hits the world. In France, many workers are unemployed and live in poverty.

In 1936, the left-wing parties unite in the "Popular Front" and win the elections. Léon Blum becomes head of government.

Straight away, millions of workers go on cheerful [strikes]: they occupy the factories, singing and dancing, to demand better working conditions.

The government and employers sign agreements, then laws are passed:
- [paid holidays]: for the first time, all employees are entitled to two weeks of paid holiday a year!
- the working week is cut to 40 hours;
- wages go up;
- school becomes compulsory until 14.

In summer 1936, thousands of working families discover the sea or the mountains for the first time, thanks to cheap train tickets. They set off on bikes, on tandems, by train, with tents.

Another new thing: three women join the government, including the scientist Irène Joliot-Curie. That's surprising, because women still don't have the right to vote!

The Popular Front shows that democracy isn't only about the right to vote, but also about [social rights]: the right to rest, to decent working conditions and to a dignified life.

title: 1940: the Republic abolished
text:
In 1939, the Second World War begins. In June 1940, the French army is defeated by Nazi Germany. A large part of France is occupied.

On 10 July 1940, in Vichy, the deputies and senators give full powers to Marshal Pétain, an old hero of the First World War. Only 80 members of parliament vote against.

Pétain abolishes the Republic. The new regime is called the "French State". The motto "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity" is replaced by "Work, Family, Homeland". There are no more elections, newspapers are [censored|censorship] and opponents are arrested. It is a [dictatorship].

The Vichy regime collaborates with Nazi Germany. It passes laws against Jews and takes part in arresting them. Tens of thousands of Jews in France, including thousands of children, are deported to Nazi extermination camps.

But some French people refuse. On 18 June 1940, from London, General de Gaulle calls for the fight to continue. In France, women and men join the [Resistance]: they hide people who are being hunted, write secret newspapers and carry out sabotage. Many pay with their lives.

In 1944, France is liberated. General de Gaulle's government restores the Republic and its freedoms.

This period reminds us that democracy and freedoms are fragile, and that we must defend them.

title: Women win the right to vote
text:
In 1848, universal suffrage was proclaimed... but only for men. For almost a century, half of the French population, women, could neither vote nor be elected.

Yet women fought for this right. They are called [suffragettes]. In France, in 1880, Hubertine Auclert refuses to pay her taxes: "I don't vote, I don't pay!" She organises protests and founds a newspaper. Other women, like Louise Weiss in the 1930s, release balloons, chain themselves to railings or give forget-me-not flowers to deputies, with the slogan "Don't forget me!".

Several times, the deputies vote in favour of women's suffrage, but the senators refuse.

Other countries are far ahead: New Zealand as early as 1893, Finland in 1906, the United Kingdom in 1918, the United States in 1920.

During the Second World War, many women took part in the Resistance. On 21 April 1944, an [ordinance] from General de Gaulle's government, then in Algiers, declares: "Women can vote and be elected under the same conditions as men."

On 29 April 1945, French women vote for the first time, in local elections. In October 1945, 33 women are elected to parliament.

Suffrage finally becomes truly universal. It took almost 100 years after 1848!

title: The Fourth Republic and new rights
The Fifth Republic
Electing the president by direct universal suffrage
text:
At the start of the Fifth Republic, the president is elected by about 80,000 "grand electors": deputies, senators and local councillors.

General de Gaulle wants the president to be chosen directly by all citizens, so that he has more strength against the political parties.

In 1962, he proposes a referendum. On 28 October 1962, the French say yes: from now on, the President of the Republic will be elected by [direct universal suffrage], meaning by all voters.

The first election of this kind takes place in December 1965. For the first time, candidates campaign on television. Charles de Gaulle is re-elected in the second round against François Mitterrand.

How does the presidential election work?
- There are two rounds. In the first round, there are several candidates. If none gets more than half the votes, the top two face each other in the second round, two weeks later.
- At first, the president was elected for 7 years. Since 2002, it has been 5 years. You can't serve more than two terms in a row.

Voting takes place at a [polling station], often in a school or town hall. You take ballot papers, go into the [voting booth] so nobody can see your choice, put your ballot in an envelope, then into the ballot box. You sign the list, and the official says: "A voté!" ("Has voted!").

Today, the presidential election is the one in which the most French people vote.

title: Women gain their independence
text:
Women won the right to vote in 1944. Yet in everyday life, a married woman was still not her husband's equal!

Napoleon's Civil Code said that a wife owed obedience to her husband. Even in the 1960s, a husband could still object to his wife working, and a married woman could not open a bank account on her own.

On 13 July 1965, a law changes this: a married woman can now have a job and open a bank account without her husband's permission.

Other laws follow to move [equality] between women and men forward:
- in 1970, "parental authority" replaces the father's authority: father and mother decide together for their children;
- in 1972, a law says that for equal work, pay must be equal between women and men;
- since 1975, schools have mixed boys and girls: this is called [co-education].

Famous women marked this period, like Simone Veil, Minister of Health in 1974, then the first president of the elected European Parliament.

But inequalities still remain today: on average, women earn less than men and still do most of the housework. Equality between women and men is a fight that goes on.

title: Voting at 18
text:
Until 1974, in France, you became an [adult] in the eyes of the law at 21. Before that age, you couldn't vote, or marry or sign certain contracts without your parents' agreement.

Yet since the 1960s, young people had wanted to take a bigger part in society. In May 1968, huge demonstrations by students and workers showed their wish for change.

The new president, Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, elected in 1974, decides to lower the age of majority. On 5 July 1974, a law sets the age of majority at 18. About 2.4 million young people become voters at once!

Becoming an adult at 18 means having new rights: voting, standing in some elections, taking your driving test, signing a job contract...

But it also means new responsibilities: you alone are responsible for your actions before the law.

Today, at 18, you are automatically put on the electoral roll if you registered for national service census at 16. You receive your voter card at a citizenship ceremony at the town hall, with a citizen's booklet.

Some people now suggest lowering the voting age to 16, as in Austria. What do you think?

title: The abolition of the death penalty
text:
For a very long time in France, criminals convicted of the worst crimes could be sentenced to death. Since the Revolution, they were executed by guillotine.

As early as the 19th century, writers like Victor Hugo called for the abolition of the [death penalty]. Hugo wrote that it was "the special and eternal sign of barbarism".

In 1981, François Mitterrand is elected President of the Republic. He had promised to abolish the death penalty, even though most French people were still in favour of it.

The Minister of Justice, the lawyer Robert Badinter, defends the bill before the deputies on 17 September 1981, in a speech that has become famous. He explains that justice must not kill, that there is always a risk of executing an innocent person, and that the death penalty does not prevent crime.

The law of 9 October 1981 abolishes the death penalty in France. The last execution had taken place in 1977.

In 2007, the abolition was written into the Constitution: "No one may be sentenced to death."

Today, more than two-thirds of the world's countries have abolished the death penalty, in law or in practice. All the countries of the European Union have abolished it. But it still exists in some countries.

Robert Badinter was laid to rest in the Panthéon in 2025, to honour his fight for justice and human rights.

title: Parity: as many women as men
text:
Even after 1944, women had the right to be elected, but very few were. In 1997, only about 11% of deputies were women!

To change this, the Constitution was amended in 1999: it says that the law "promotes equal access for women and men to elected office".

On 6 June 2000, a law on [parity] is passed. For many elections, lists of candidates must include as many women as men, alternating them: a woman, a man, a woman, a man...

For elections to département councils, since 2015, people even vote for a pair: one woman and one man elected together!

Thanks to these laws, things have changed a lot: today, the councils of towns and regions have almost as many women as men. In the National Assembly, about 36% of deputies are women.

Women have held very high offices: Édith Cresson, the first woman Prime Minister in 1991, or Yaël Braun-Pivet, the first woman President of the National Assembly in 2022.

But there is still a way to go: France has never had a woman President of the Republic, and mayors are still mostly men.

title: A citizen's rights and duties
Who decides in the Republic?
text:
In a [democracy], the people choose their leaders through elections. Powers are separated so that nobody has all the power, as the philosopher Montesquieu wanted.

Who does what in the Fifth Republic?

- The President of the Republic is elected for 5 years by all citizens. He or she lives and works at the Élysée Palace in Paris, appoints the Prime Minister, leads foreign policy and is head of the armed forces.
- The government, led by the Prime Minister and made up of ministers (Education, Health...), applies the laws and runs the country day to day.
- [Parliament] votes the laws and checks the government's work. It has two houses: the National Assembly, with 577 deputies elected by the citizens, and the Senate, with 348 senators elected by local councillors.
- Judges deliver justice independently.
- The Constitutional Council checks that laws respect the Constitution.

The Republic is also close to home:
- the town is run by the town council and the [mayor], elected for 6 years. The town hall looks after primary schools, canteens, streets, parks...
- the département looks after secondary schools (collèges) and social help;
- the region looks after high schools (lycées) and transport.

There are also European elections, because France is part of the European Union.

All these elected people are there to serve the citizens. If they don't do their job well, voters can choose someone else at the next election.
